title: Paired Expressions
subtitle: Two-part connectors for options, additions and opinions.
objectives: Use either … or and neither … nor to offer and rule out options
Use both … and and not only … but also to add information with emphasis
Use rather … than and whether … or for preference and indifference
Choose the right verb form after a paired subject

content.intro: You already use and, but and or on their own. Paired expressions work in two halves, and each first half commits you to one specific second half — pick the wrong partner and the sentence breaks. This lesson drills the six pairs on the B2 sheet, plus the verb agreement rule that catches most students out.
content.explanation: A paired (or correlative) expression joins two elements with two linking words that always travel together: either … or, neither … nor, both … and, not only … but also, rather … than and whether … or. Two things matter: choosing the right partner word, and putting the same kind of element on each side — two nouns, two verbs or two clauses, never one of each.

rules.heading: a) Options: either … or / neither … nor
rules.body:
• either … or presents two possibilities, one of which applies: You can have either the soup or the salad.
  • neither … nor is the negative version — it rules both out: I drink neither coffee nor tea.
  • nor is already negative, so the verb stays positive: Neither this nor that works (not doesn't work).

rules.heading: b) Addition: both … and / not only … but also
rules.body:
• both … and adds two elements neutrally: Both you and I know the answer.
  • not only … but also adds a second, more striking point: I'd like not only the bread but also the cheese.
  • When not only opens the clause, the subject and auxiliary invert: Not only was she talented, but she was also kind.

rules.heading: c) Preference: rather … than
rules.body:
• would rather … than states a preference, with a bare infinitive on both sides: I'd rather walk than wait for the bus.
  • No to and no -ing: not rather to walk than waiting.

rules.heading: d) Indifference: whether … or
rules.body:
• whether … or says the outcome is the same either way: I'll go, whether it rains or not.
  • It can join phrases as well as clauses: Music is good, whether at home or in the car.
  • Only whether — not if — works directly before or not and before an infinitive: whether or not to accept.

rules.heading: e) Verb agreement after a paired subject
rules.body:
• both … and is always plural: Both the cat and the dog want to go outside.
  • With either … or, neither … nor and not only … but also, the verb agrees with the nearer noun: Neither the kids nor the teacher is ready. / Neither the teacher nor the kids are ready.

examples: You can have either the soup or the salad.
Neither this nor that option works for me.
Both you and I know the answer.
Not only was she talented, but she was also kind.
I'd rather walk than wait for the bus.
I'll go, whether it rains or not.
Neither the kids nor the teacher is ready.

commonMistakes.wrong: Either the bus or the train are fine.
commonMistakes.right: Either the bus or the train is fine.
commonMistakes.why: After either … or the verb agrees with the nearer noun — here the singular "train".

commonMistakes.wrong: Both the manager and the staff was informed.
commonMistakes.right: Both the manager and the staff were informed.
commonMistakes.why: both … and always makes a plural subject, however singular each half looks.

commonMistakes.wrong: Neither of us didn't know about it.
commonMistakes.right: Neither of us knew about it.
commonMistakes.why: neither / nor is already negative — adding didn't makes a double negative.

commonMistakes.wrong: I'd rather to stay home than going out.
commonMistakes.right: I'd rather stay home than go out.
commonMistakes.why: rather … than takes a bare infinitive on both sides — no "to", no "-ing".

commonMistakes.wrong: Not only she was late, but she also forgot the file.
commonMistakes.right: Not only was she late, but she also forgot the file.
commonMistakes.why: When not only opens the clause, the subject and auxiliary invert.

commonMistakes.wrong: I haven't decided if or not to accept.
commonMistakes.right: I haven't decided whether or not to accept.
commonMistakes.why: Only whether can sit directly before "or not" and before an infinitive — "if" cannot.

exercises.title: Complete Both Halves
exercises.instructions: Type the missing word in each gap. Both halves of the pair have been removed.

items.prompt: ___ the flight ___ the hotel has been confirmed yet, so we may have to postpone.
items.explanation: Both options are ruled out, so the negative pair neither … nor is needed. "Has" is singular because it agrees with the nearer noun, "hotel".

items.prompt: You can pay ___ by card ___ in cash — the shop accepts both.
items.explanation: Two available possibilities, one of which you choose: either … or.

items.prompt: ___ the design ___ the price impressed the client, which is why they signed the same day.
items.explanation: Two things added neutrally: both … and. It always makes a plural subject.

items.prompt: ___ only did the team miss the deadline, ___ they also went over budget.
items.explanation: not only … but also adds a second, worse point. Note the inversion already in place: "did the team miss", not "the team missed".

items.prompt: I'd ___ send an email ___ call him this late.
items.explanation: would rather … than states a preference, with a bare infinitive on each side: "send" … "call".

items.prompt: We're going ahead ___ the others join us ___ not.
items.explanation: The plan doesn't change either way — that's whether … or. "If" cannot be used directly before "or not".

items.prompt: She speaks ___ Spanish ___ Portuguese, which is why we booked an interpreter.
items.explanation: Both languages are ruled out. "Nor" is already negative, so the verb "speaks" stays positive.

items.prompt: The role demands ___ technical skill ___ patience, and very few candidates have both.
items.explanation: Two requirements added together: both … and.

items.prompt: We'll have to ___ cut the budget ___ extend the deadline — there's no third option.
items.explanation: Two alternatives, one of which must happen: either … or.

items.prompt: ___ you agree ___ not, the new policy takes effect on Monday.
items.explanation: The outcome is the same either way, so whether … or is correct. "If you agree or not" is not standard English.

exercises.title: Verb Agreement After a Paired Subject
exercises.instructions: Choose the verb form that agrees correctly with the paired subject.

items.prompt: Both the director and the producer ___ at the premiere.
items.explanation: both … and is always plural, so the verb is "were" — even though each half is singular.

items.prompt: Neither the players nor the coach ___ willing to comment.
items.explanation: With neither … nor the verb agrees with the nearer noun, and "the coach" is singular.

items.prompt: Neither the coach nor the players ___ willing to comment.
items.explanation: Same rule, reversed order: the nearer noun is now the plural "the players", so the verb is plural.

items.prompt: Either the twins or their mother ___ the spare keys.
items.explanation: The nearer noun is the singular "their mother", so "has" is correct after either … or.

items.prompt: Not only the windows but also the door ___ been left open.
items.explanation: not only … but also follows the nearer-noun rule too, and "the door" is singular.

items.prompt: Both the report and the invoice ___ missing from the file.
items.explanation: both … and makes a plural subject, so "are".

items.prompt: Either the interns or the supervisor ___ to sign the form.
items.explanation: The nearer noun is the singular "the supervisor".

items.prompt: Neither my parents nor my sister ___ seen the message.
items.explanation: The nearer noun is the singular "my sister", so "has seen".

items.prompt: Not only the students but also the teacher ___ surprised by the result.
items.explanation: The nearer noun is the singular "the teacher".

items.prompt: Both the engine and the brakes ___ checked last week.
items.explanation: both … and is plural, so "were checked".

exercises.title: Correct the Mistakes
exercises.instructions: Each sentence has one error in its paired expression. Write the corrected sentence.

items.incorrect: Either the manager or the assistants is available at the moment.
answer: Either the manager or the assistants are available at the moment.
items.explanation: After either … or the verb agrees with the nearer noun, and "the assistants" is plural.

items.incorrect: Neither the email nor the phone call didn't reach him.
answer: Neither the email nor the phone call reached him.
items.explanation: neither … nor is already negative, so "didn't" makes a double negative.

items.incorrect: I'd rather to walk than taking the bus.
answer: I'd rather walk than take the bus.
I would rather walk than take the bus.
items.explanation: rather … than needs a bare infinitive on both sides: "walk" … "take".

items.incorrect: Both the software and the hardware needs updating.
answer: Both the software and the hardware need updating.
items.explanation: both … and is plural, so the verb loses its -s.

items.incorrect: Not only she missed the meeting, but she also lost the file.
answer: Not only did she miss the meeting, but she also lost the file.
Not only did she miss the meeting but she also lost the file.
items.explanation: When not only opens the clause, the subject and auxiliary invert: "did she miss".

items.incorrect: I haven't decided if or not to accept the offer.
answer: I haven't decided whether or not to accept the offer.
I haven't decided whether to accept the offer or not.
items.explanation: Only whether can sit directly before "or not" and before an infinitive.

items.incorrect: Either you apologise and you leave.
answer: Either you apologise or you leave.
items.explanation: "Either" must be answered by "or", never by "and".

items.incorrect: Neither the design or the price was acceptable.
answer: Neither the design nor the price was acceptable.
items.explanation: "Neither" must be answered by "nor", not "or".

items.incorrect: Both the twins as well as their cousin are coming.
answer: Both the twins and their cousin are coming.
items.explanation: "Both" must be answered by "and" — mixing it with "as well as" breaks the pair.

items.incorrect: Not only he was rude, but he was also dishonest.
answer: Not only was he rude, but he was also dishonest.
Not only was he rude but he was also dishonest.
items.explanation: not only at the start of a clause forces inversion: "was he rude".

items.incorrect: We would rather cancelling the trip than risk it.
answer: We would rather cancel the trip than risk it.
items.explanation: After "would rather" use a bare infinitive, not an -ing form.

items.incorrect: He can play both the piano and also the violin.
answer: He can play both the piano and the violin.
items.explanation: "Both … and" is already complete — "also" is redundant here.

items.incorrect: Whether you like it and not, the rules have changed.
answer: Whether you like it or not, the rules have changed.
Whether you like it or not the rules have changed.
items.explanation: "Whether" is answered by "or", giving the fixed phrase "whether or not".

items.incorrect: Not only the roof but also the walls was damaged.
answer: Not only the roof but also the walls were damaged.
items.explanation: The verb agrees with the nearer noun, and "the walls" is plural.

items.incorrect: Either the keys are in the drawer or in the car.
answer: The keys are either in the drawer or in the car.
items.explanation: Put the same kind of element on each side of the pair: here two place phrases, so "either" moves after "are".

exercises.title: Choose the Missing Half
exercises.instructions: Pick the word that completes the pair.

items.prompt: You can have either the soup ___ the salad.
items.explanation: "Either" is always answered by "or".

items.prompt: I drink neither coffee ___ tea.
items.explanation: "Neither" is always answered by "nor".

items.prompt: Both the cat ___ the dog want to go outside.
items.explanation: "Both" is always answered by "and", and the verb is plural.

items.prompt: Not only was she talented, ___ she was also kind.
items.explanation: The pair is "not only … but also".

items.prompt: I'd rather walk ___ wait for the bus.
items.explanation: "Rather" is answered by "than" — not "then", which is about time.

items.prompt: I'll go, ___ it rains or not.
items.explanation: Only "whether" works before "or not"; "if" cannot be used here.

items.prompt: ___ the kids nor the teacher is ready.
items.explanation: "Nor" in the second half tells you the first half must be "neither".

items.prompt: We need ___ more time or more staff.
items.explanation: "Or" in the second half tells you the first half must be "either".

items.prompt: The film was ___ only long but also confusing.
items.explanation: The pair opens with "not only".

items.prompt: ___ the cost and the delay annoyed the client.
items.explanation: "And" in the second half tells you the first half must be "both".

exercises.title: Which Pair Fits the Meaning?
exercises.instructions: Read the situation, then choose the sentence that actually says it.

items.prompt: The kitchen has run out of fish and out of steak. Which sentence reports that?
options: They serve neither fish nor steak tonight.
They serve either fish or steak tonight.
They serve both fish and steak tonight.
items.explanation: Both options are unavailable, so only the negative pair is true. The other two claim something is on offer.

items.prompt: The 9:00 train and the 10:00 train suit you equally well. Which sentence says that?
options: I'd rather take the 9:00 than the 10:00.
I don't mind whether I take the 9:00 or the 10:00.
I'll take whether the 9:00 or the 10:00.
items.explanation: whether … or expresses indifference. The first states a preference, and the third is ungrammatical — "whether" needs a clause after it.

items.prompt: You want to stress that the report was late — and, worse, inaccurate. Which sentence does that?
options: Not only was the report late, but it was also inaccurate.
Either the report was late or it was inaccurate.
The report was neither late nor inaccurate.
items.explanation: not only … but also adds a second, stronger criticism. The others offer alternatives or deny both faults.

items.prompt: You prefer walking to driving. Which sentence is correct?
options: I'd rather walk than to drive.
items.explanation: rather … than takes a bare infinitive on both sides — no "to" and no "-ing".

items.prompt: Two rooms are free, but you may book only one of them. Which sentence says that?
options: You can take either the single or the double.
You can take both the single and the double.
You can take neither the single nor the double.
items.explanation: either … or offers a choice of one. The second gives you both, the third gives you none.

items.prompt: Ana was promoted, and Tom was promoted too. Which sentence reports that?
options: Either Ana or Tom was promoted.
Neither Ana nor Tom was promoted.
Both Ana and Tom were promoted.
items.explanation: both … and adds the two together, and takes the plural "were".

items.prompt: The match will be played no matter what the weather does. Which sentence says that?
options: The match will go ahead whether it rains or not.
The match will go ahead either it rains or not.
The match will go ahead rather it rains than not.
items.explanation: Only whether … or can introduce "or not" like this; the other two are not possible English.

items.prompt: A colleague offers you tea or coffee, but you drink neither. Which reply is correct?
options: Neither, thanks — I don't drink either.
Either, thanks — I don't drink neither.
items.explanation: "Neither" rules both out. "I don't drink either" keeps a single negative — "don't drink neither" is a double negative.

items.prompt: You want to say the shop takes cards and cash. Which sentence is correct?
options: The shop accepts both cards and cash.
The shop accepts neither cards nor cash.
The shop accepts rather cards than cash.
items.explanation: both … and adds two accepted options together.

items.prompt: Which sentence correctly puts the same kind of element on each side of the pair?
options: She not only writes the code but also the documentation.
She writes not only the code but also the documentation.
She writes not only the code but she also the documentation.
items.explanation: "Not only" and "but also" should each be followed by the same kind of element — here two noun phrases, so both sit after the verb "writes".

exercises.title: Build the Sentence
exercises.instructions: Tap the words in the right order, following the hint in each prompt.

items.prompt: Not only / she / apologise / did / but / also / offered to pay
items.explanation: Not only + inverted auxiliary + bare infinitive ("did she apologise"), then "but … also" before the second verb.

items.prompt: Use the singular verb "was": Neither / the landlord / nor / the tenants / aware of the leak / was
items.explanation: The singular "was" only agrees if the singular noun is nearer, so "the landlord" has to follow "nor".

items.prompt: Say you prefer walking: rather / walk home / I / than / would / wait for a taxi
items.explanation: would rather + bare infinitive, than + bare infinitive. The preferred action comes first.

items.prompt: Mention the manager first: were informed of the change / Both / the team / and / the manager
items.explanation: both … and takes the plural "were", whichever noun you name first.

items.prompt: Begin with "Whether": the policy / Whether / or not / takes effect on Monday / you agree
items.explanation: "Whether … or not" forms a complete clause, which can come first and is followed by the main clause.

exercises.title: Guided Production
exercises.instructions: Write your own sentence for each prompt. There's no single correct answer — a model answer is shown for comparison after you submit.

items.prompt: Write one sentence about your week using NOT ONLY … BUT ALSO, starting with "Not only" (remember the inversion).
items.modelAnswer: Not only did I finish the report, but I also cleared my entire inbox.

items.prompt: Write one sentence with NEITHER … NOR about two things you never do.
items.modelAnswer: I neither smoke nor drink coffee after midday.

items.prompt: Write one sentence with WHETHER … OR about a decision that doesn't depend on anything.
items.modelAnswer: We're launching on Monday, whether the final designs arrive or not.

items.prompt: Write one sentence with BOTH … AND about two things the job you want requires. Check your verb is plural.
items.modelAnswer: Both fluent English and solid data skills are essential for the role.

items.prompt: Write one sentence with WOULD RATHER … THAN about a choice you face this week. Use a bare infinitive on each side.
items.modelAnswer: I'd rather take the early train than spend an hour in traffic.

summary: The six pairs: either … or, neither … nor, both … and, not only … but also, rather … than, whether … or.
Put the same kind of element on each side — two nouns, two verbs or two clauses, never a mix.
both … and is always plural; either … or, neither … nor and not only … but also agree with the nearer noun.
nor is already negative, rather … than takes bare infinitives, and not only at the start of a clause forces inversion.
